# What changes now {#sec-ch14}

Predictions about AI often turn out wrong, so this last chapter stays with three things: what this book has shown, what it suggests, and what nobody knows yet.

::: {.goals}
- See the decision layer as a separate part of an AI system.
- Understand why cheaper decisions can mean more work for people.
- Leave with a clear plan for your first decision.
:::

## A separate layer for decisions

For the last few years, the usual AI system has been one big model doing everything: reading, deciding, writing and using tools, all through text.

![Two ways to build an AI system. Left: one model does everything as text. Right: each layer does one job. An LLM reads and writes, a decision layer answers typed questions with probabilities, a policy turns those into actions, and tools, logs and people sit underneath.](/figures/ch29/stack.pdf){#fig-stack}

The right side of @fig-stack shows the design this book has been building, chapter by chapter. The LLM does what only an LLM can do: read anything and write for people. The decision layer answers small, clear questions in one step, with probabilities we can check. The policy, your own rules, draws the lines based on the cost of mistakes and the size of the team. And at the bottom, tools take actions and people review. Each part is smaller than the whole system, can be tested on its own, and can be replaced without rebuilding everything else. So when a better LLM or a cheaper decision model appears, you can change one part and keep the rest. This is why we think the design will last.

::: {.keyidea}
**Give each part of the system one job.** The LLM reads and writes, the decision model decides, your rules choose the action, and people decide what mistakes cost.
:::

## Cheaper decisions, more decisions

In 1865, the economist William Stanley Jevons noticed something surprising about coal [@jevons1865]. James Watt's steam engine produced much more work from each tonne of coal. People expected Britain to use less coal. Instead, it used much more, because cheaper coal power was now used for many more things. We have seen the same with mobile data in India: when data became very cheap, people did not just save money; they started watching videos all day. This pattern is called the **Jevons paradox**. The name Jev comes from Jevons, and this time the "coal" is decisions.

A check is worth doing only when the loss it can prevent is bigger than what the check costs, and when it can be done in time. Today a company makes a few thousand careful decisions per day. But it *could* make millions: one for every email, every login and every line in its computer logs. Checking any one of these is worth only a tiny amount of money. At the example LLM price of \${{< num ch19 llm_price f5 >}} per decision, almost none are worth checking. At Jev's reported price of \${{< num ch19 jev_price f6 >}}, many are.

Where does the bill change? For checks a company already does, cheaper decisions mean many more checks (in our example, {{< num ch19 decisions_ratio int >}} times more), but the total bill still goes *down*, because each check is so cheap. The bill goes up only when cheap decisions make *new* kinds of checks worth doing, such as checking every file that anyone shares outside the company.

::: {.keyidea}
**When decisions become cheap, we make many more of them.** When mobile data became cheap in India, people did not save money; they used far more data. Cheap decisions will be used for many new tasks in the same way.
:::

![Alerts sent to a person per day, under two rules (illustrative). A rule that flags a fixed share of what the model looks at grows with the number of decisions, and at Jev volumes it sends far more than the team can handle. A cost-based threshold, which flags only when the expected loss is larger than the cost of a review, barely moves.](/figures/ch19/flags.pdf){#fig-flags}

There is a hidden cost: more decisions also means more cases sent to people. Consider a rule that seemed fine when there were few decisions: "send the top 0.1% to a person". It sends {{< num ch19 flags_top_llm int >}} cases per day, which the team, able to check {{< num ch19 capacity int >}}, can handle. At the new, higher volume, the same rule sends {{< num ch19 flags_top_jev int >}} per day, even though nobody changed it (@fig-flags). A rule based on cost, which sends a case to a person only when the loss it may cause is higher than the cost of checking it, sends {{< num ch19 flags_cost_jev int >}} per day at both volumes.

::: {.keyidea}
**As the number of cases grows, set the line by cost, not by percentage.** "Send the top 0.1% to a person" sends more and more cases as volume grows. "Send it when the possible loss is more than the cost of checking" stays steady.
:::

## What becomes valuable

If deciding becomes cheap, what becomes rare and valuable? Good human judgement about the decision itself. Someone still has to decide what each mistake costs, where the thresholds should be, how many cases the team can review, and whether the probabilities are still correct this week. No model can do this for you. This is why the first chapters of this book, about probability, correct numbers and costs, are the foundation. They make the difference between a system that makes a million cheap decisions well and one that makes a million cheap mistakes.

![Skills that matter more when decisions get cheap, and skills that matter less on their own, with the chapters that teach each.](/figures/ch29/skills.pdf){#fig-skills}

::: {.keyidea}
**When machines decide cheaply, human judgement becomes more valuable.** Someone must still decide what each mistake costs, where the lines are, and how many people are needed. No model can do this for you.
:::

Many things are still unknown: whether a System One model's numbers are correct on your data, how it changes between versions, how it behaves when attackers write the input, and what the final prices will be. None of these is a reason to wait. You can check its numbers on your own past cases this week. You can handle version changes with a fixed version and daily monitoring. You can check prices in a spreadsheet. And this design does not depend on any one company: if your system sends a clear question, gets back a probability, and keeps its rules in your own program, you can move to a different model in a day.

![Open questions, and what you can do about each today.](/figures/ch29/unknowns.pdf){#fig-unknowns}

::: {.keyidea}
**Build your system so that every part can be measured, adjusted and replaced.** Then you are safe even if a company changes its prices or its model, because you can switch to another one in a day.
:::

## What to do on Monday

If you do only one thing after reading this book, make a list of every decision your system makes, and count how often each one happens. Most people are surprised by how many there are, and how many are small, clear and frequent.

![A first three months, one decision at a time.](/figures/ch29/monday.pdf){#fig-monday}

Then choose *one* decision. Collect a few hundred past cases with known answers and check whether the model's numbers are correct. Put a cost on each type of mistake and draw the lines. Run it in shadow mode. Switch it on with a rule for failures, random checks and daily monitoring. Then move to the next decision. This is not exciting work, but it is how every system in this book became better.

::: {.breaks}
This chapter is the least certain part of the book. The cost and speed numbers are examples, and Jev's numbers are as reported by the company during early access. The idea that every AI system will soon have a separate decision layer is our opinion based on the evidence, not a proven fact. It could be wrong if general models become fast and well calibrated enough. Even then, everything about costs, thresholds and calibration will still apply.
:::

::: {.threshold}
Take the most frequent decision in your own system. What does a wrong "yes" cost? What does a wrong "no" cost? Where should the threshold be? And how will you know, one month from now, whether the probabilities behind it are still correct?

(There is no answer at the back of the book for this one. If you can answer all four questions, you have learned what this book set out to teach.)
:::

![The whole book as one story.](/figures/ch29/journey.pdf){#fig-journey}

Alan Turing ended his most famous paper with a line that suits this moment: "We can only see a short distance ahead, but we can see plenty there that needs to be done" [@turing1950].

::: {.exercises}
1. Make a decision list for one system you know: every decision, how often it happens, what a mistake costs, and who is responsible for it.
:::
